read.sections.0.text.back: Look at the woven bag in the evidence. The seller says the bag was made to carry food and books. That is its practical use. Its owner says her/his aunt gave the bag to her/him when she/he started studying at a new school, so the bag also holds memories. The bag's maker, that is, a craft group, learned the pattern from older weavers. For them, the bag shows a skill. There is only one bag, but each person sees it from a different perspective. To understand an object, you need to know the object's context: who made it, who uses it, and why.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Objects carry meaning all over the world
read.sections.1.heading.source: Objects carry meaning around the world

read.sections.1.text.back: Many communities make objects that have cultural meaning. In Ghana, weavers make kente cloth from narrow strips of cloth, which are then sewn together. Many kente patterns have names, and some of those names come from proverbs or events in history. In Indonesia, people decorate batik cloth with hot wax and dye. Batik is used throughout life, from cloth for carrying a baby to clothing for wedding ceremonies. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups of people often make it together, and the cloth is used in wedding ceremonies and other big events.

Batik is used through life, from cloths that carry babies to clothes for weddings. In the Pacific, in places such as Tonga and Fiji, people beat tree bark to make tapa cloth. Groups often make it together, and it is used at weddings and other big events.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Ask first before explaining an object
read.sections.2.heading.source: Ask before you explain an object

read.sections.2.text.back: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag only said “Everyday carrying bag”. That label is correct, but it does not mention memories and skill. Guessing the meaning of the pattern is also a mistake. A label that calls the pattern a symbol for the whole community, without any source, is a weak label. People in one group might not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from makers and users. That label states what we know and what we still need to ask.
read.sections.2.text.source: A museum label tells visitors about an object. The first label for the bag says only “Everyday carrying bag”. That is true, but it misses the memory and the skill. It is also a mistake to guess what the pattern means. A label that calls the pattern a symbol of a whole community, with no source, is weak. People in one group may not all see an object in the same way. A better label uses evidence from the makers and users. It says what we know and what we still need to ask.

That label also states what we still need to ask.

Also check 'Ramai orang biasa memakainya': it could be read as 'many people usually wore it' instead of 'many ordinary people wore it'. 'orang kebanyakan' (commoners) is clearer if needed. watch.summary.back: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This video looks at three everyday objects from that museum. The first object is a small green jar/vase from China. In olden times, people in the Philippines traded to get jars/vases and bowls from China. Most of them were just plain, but this jar has two dragons on it. The second object is the salakot, that is, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it [or: Many people usually wore it]. But some salakot were decorated with shells and silver for important people. The third object is a small piece of cloth called a sapu tangan (handkerchief). If you look at it carefully, you can see a sad poem sewn on it. This video states that materials and skill make an object valuable. But the story and context around it make the object more special.
watch.summary.source: This short video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. It looks at three everyday objects from the museum. The first is a small green pot from China. Long ago, people in the Philippines traded for Chinese pots and bowls. Most were plain, but this one has two dragons on it. The second is the salakot, a wide hat woven from plants. Many ordinary people wore it. But some salakot were decorated with shell and silver for important people. The third is a small cloth called a handkerchief. If you look closely, you can see a sad poem sewn into it. The video says the materials and the skill make an object valuable. But the stories and context around it make it even more special.
